transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi… thanks. I guess what brings me in is that I’ve been feeling like I just can’t settle in my own body anymore. Like, it’s not just being a little fidgety or impatient — it’s this constant internal restlessness, especially when I’m supposed to sit down and do something calm and practical, like paperwork or going over household plans with someone.

Those are the moments where it really stands out, because I know I’m supposed to just sit there, listen, think through things, maybe fill something out or make decisions, and instead I feel like I’m almost crawling out of my skin. I’ll be sitting there, but inside I feel like I need to get up or shift around or do something else. It makes even normal shared household stuff feel harder than it should, and it’s been frustrating enough that I thought I should finally talk to someone about it.
Did this restless feeling start after you began taking a medication or changed the dose of one?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t have a clear memory of it starting right after a medication change or anything like that. I mean, I can try to think back, but nothing jumps out as, “Oh, this began when I started taking X,” or “it got worse when the dose changed.”

It feels more like something I’ve been noticing in certain situations, especially when I’m expected to sit still and focus, rather than something I can tie to a specific pill or dose change. But I might need to look back more carefully if that’s important.
When you were a child, did you often have trouble sitting still in class?

Yes… looking back, I think it was already there when I was pretty young, especially in elementary school. At the time I don’t think anyone framed it that way exactly, like “trouble sitting still,” but there were a lot of signs.

I was sort of known as the girl with the messy desk — papers crammed everywhere, things falling out, permission slips forgotten or lost at the bottom of my backpack. And I do remember teacher notes coming home, or comments on report cards, saying I talked out of turn or interrupted, or that I seemed like I couldn’t stay in my seat when I was supposed to. I wasn’t trying to be difficult, at least not how I remember it. It felt more like I just… couldn’t quite contain myself the way other kids seemed to.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying about many different things?

I’m not sure I’d describe it as worrying about many different things, at least not in the way I think you mean. I do get caught up in thoughts sometimes, but it’s hard for me to tell if that’s “worry” exactly or more like my mind just keeps jumping around and not settling.

I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there all day consumed by fears about everything, if that’s what you’re asking. It’s more… I can get stuck thinking through practical stuff or replaying things, but I don’t know that I have this broad, constant worry across lots of areas. I may be overthinking the wording, sorry — I just don’t want to say yes if it’s not really that.
Do you get unwanted thoughts that keep coming back even when you try to push them away?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I do have thoughts that repeat, but I don’t know if I’d call them “unwanted thoughts” in the sense of something intrusive or disturbing that I’m trying really hard to push away and it keeps forcing itself back in.

It’s more like my mind can get snagged on something, and then I’ll circle around it, but I’m not sure that’s the same thing. If you mean thoughts that feel alien or really upsetting, like they pop in against my will and I can’t get rid of them, I don’t think I’ve noticed that in a clear way. At least nothing that stands out to me as a major pattern.
Do these attention or restlessness problems cause significant trouble in your work, school, or relationships?

Yes, it does. I mean… I wish I could say it was just annoying or just something I notice internally, but it has had real consequences.

The biggest place I see it now is at home and in the volunteer things I’m involved with. People will ask me to handle something, and I fully intend to do it — I’m not saying yes casually — but then I’ll lose track of the steps, or forget to follow through, or realize too late that I missed some piece of it. And after that happens enough times, people start to sort of… work around me, I guess. Or they check up on me more, which makes me feel embarrassed, because I know they’re doing it because they can’t totally count on me.

I’ve actually had to step back from some responsibilities because I kept letting things fall through even when I was trying really hard. That’s the part that feels upsetting — it’s not that I don’t care. I care a lot. But the end result is still that things don’t get done reliably, and it affects other people’s trust in me.
When you feel this inner restlessness, do you also find yourself pacing or unable to stay seated?

Yes… I think that’s actually one of the main reasons I’m here. It’s like I can’t settle in my own body anymore, especially when I’m supposed to just sit quietly and deal with something that needs sustained attention, like paperwork or going over household plans with someone.

I don’t know if I’m always literally pacing back and forth, but I definitely feel this pressure to get up, shift around, move, do something. Sitting still for those kinds of tasks can feel almost physically uncomfortable, like my body is saying, “No, we’re not doing this,” even when I know I need to. And then it makes ordinary things feel much harder than they should.
Are you currently taking any psychiatric medication?

I’m not sure how to answer that in a specific way. I don’t have a clear medication list in my head to give you right now, and I don’t want to say the wrong thing.

Do you mean anything prescribed for mood, anxiety, sleep, attention, that kind of thing? Because I can try to think it through, but off the top of my head I’m not able to give you a definite psychiatric medication name or dose.
Are you taking an antipsychotic medicine right now?

I don’t think so… but I want to be careful, because I’m not always great at remembering medication categories. Like, if you named one, I might recognize it, but just hearing “antipsychotic” as a category, I’m not immediately thinking, yes, I take that.

As far as I know, I’m not currently taking anything like that. I’d probably need to check the actual bottles or my medication list to be completely sure, because I don’t want to accidentally tell you something inaccurate.
Have you taken metoclopramide, also called Reglan, recently?

I’m not sure. Reglan doesn’t immediately ring a bell for me, and metoclopramide sounds familiar in that way where I might have heard it before, but I can’t say, “Yes, I took that recently.”

I don’t want to accidentally give you the wrong answer, because medication names are exactly the kind of thing I’m bad at keeping straight unless I’m looking at the bottle or the after-visit paperwork. If it’s something given for nausea or stomach issues, I’d have to check, honestly. Off the top of my head, I don’t know that I’ve taken it recently.
Have you started any new medicine in the last few weeks?

I’m not totally sure. I don’t think I’ve started anything new in the last few weeks, at least not that I’m remembering right now, but I’m also kind of bad at keeping track of names and timing unless I’m looking at the actual bottle or the pharmacy app.

Like, if you asked me whether I picked something up recently, I’d probably have to check, because sometimes “new” to me means a new prescription, and sometimes it’s like a refill or something I was told to take as needed, and then I don’t categorize it the same way in my head. But sitting here right now, nothing is jumping out to me as a definite new medicine.
Did this restless feeling begin soon after you started a medicine or increased the dose of one?

I’m not sure I can connect it clearly to a medicine change. What I can say is that the reason I’m here is this restless feeling, like I can’t settle in my own body anymore. It’s especially noticeable when I’m supposed to sit quietly and do things like paperwork, or when we’re trying to talk through household plans with other people.

That’s when it really stands out to me — I feel like I should be able to just sit there and focus, but instead I’m sort of crawling out of my skin. I don’t know if that started right after a medication was started or increased, because I’m honestly not great at tracking those timelines in my head.
Do you feel this need to move even during activities you enjoy?

Yes, actually, that’s one of the things that’s been bothering me because it’s not just when I’m doing boring stuff. Like, I’ll want to have a quiet evening reading next to my husband — something I actually enjoy and want to do — and I still can’t seem to just sit there peacefully.

I’ll start talking to him about random things, or humming without realizing I’m doing it, or getting up because I suddenly “need” water or a blanket or to check something. And then I notice I’m making enough noise or movement that it stops being that calm, quiet time we were trying to have. I do want to relax and read, it’s not that I don’t like it. It’s like my body or my mouth won’t fully cooperate with the quiet part.
When you get up and move around, does that restless feeling ease up?

It helps a little in the moment, I think, but it doesn’t really make it go away. Like if I’m sitting there trying to do paperwork or we’re talking through household plans, I start feeling like I can’t settle in my own body, and getting up gives me something to do with that feeling.

But then I’m not actually settled, if that makes sense. I might pace around, go into another room, shuffle papers, get a drink, come back, sit down again, and pretty quickly the same uncomfortable “I can’t just sit here” feeling is still there. It’s more like moving interrupts it for a second than actually relieves it.
Has this same inner restlessness been present since childhood?

Yes… looking back, I think it was there really early, like elementary school early. I didn’t have the words for it then, obviously, and I think adults probably just saw me as messy or chatty or not trying hard enough.

I was the girl with the disaster of a desk — papers shoved everywhere, permission slips forgotten or lost, that kind of thing. And I remember teachers sending notes home or making comments that I was talking out of turn, or that I seemed like I couldn’t stay in my seat when I was supposed to. At the time it just felt like I was always getting corrected for things other kids seemed to manage more easily.

So yes, I’d say this wasn’t something that appeared out of nowhere as an adult. It feels like it was already part of me when I was little.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptom pattern, specifically inner restlessness, has been present since childhood, which directly relates to onset before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yes… looking back, I think it was there really early, like elementary school early. I didn’t have the words for it then, obviously, and I think adults probably just saw me as messy or chatty or not trying hard enough.

I was the girl with the disaster of a desk — papers shoved everywhere, permission slips forgotten or lost, that kind of thing. And I remember teachers sending notes home or making comments that I was talking out of turn, or that I seemed like I couldn’t stay in my seat when I was supposed to. At the time it just felt like I was always getting corrected for things other kids seemed to manage more easily.

So yes, I’d say this wasn’t something that appeared out of nowhere as an adult. It feels like it was already part of me when I was little.

inference.note: Lifelong onset since childhood with clear impairing inattention/hyperactivity symptoms across settings strongly supports ADHD. Medication-induced akathisia/adverse effect is less likely given no clear temporal relationship to starting/increasing meds and no known antipsychotic/Reglan exposure.

opening_question.intent: Understand the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: History is most consistent with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, predominantly hyperactive type/including significant hyperactive-restless symptoms, with childhood onset and ongoing functional impairment. The patient describes longstanding inability to stay seated, talking out of turn, interrupting, internal restlessness, disorganization, forgetfulness, and failure to follow through, beginning in elementary school and continuing into adulthood. Medication-induced akathisia was considered but not supported by a clear temporal relationship to medication changes, and anxiety/OCD features were not endorsed as primary explanations.
